**Acquisitions**

The archive sits in the basement of the university library, three floors below special collections, behind a door marked ACQUISITIONS. The room has no windows, which is fitting. Everything in here is already past.

Mira has worked there for eleven years. Her job title, printed on her badge, is Audio Preservation Specialist. What this means in practice is that she hunts sounds the way other people hunt animals: patiently, with specialized equipment, and with a private hope that she will fail.

Because the best recordings—the only ones that matter—are made in the last days of a sound's life.

She has recorded the final steam whistle of a textile mill in Rhode Island. The last payphone on Route 9 ringing into empty air, its bell absurdly cheerful for such an obsolete instrument. The clatter of a slide projector operated by the last teacher in the county still using one—she drove four hours for that, set her microphones up between the desks while children watched her like she'd arrived from another century, which in a sense she had. She has the hum of a bowling alley's pin-setting machine, the pneumatic sigh of a bank drive-through window, the wooden knock of a hand-cranked gas pump, and forty minutes of a 1970s refrigerator, donated by a man who swore his new one was silent and considered this a tragedy.

There is a taxonomy to disappearance. Some sounds die suddenly: a factory closes, and by Tuesday the whistle is gone. Others fade slowly, thinning year by year until nobody notices they've left—like a screen door slapping shut in summer, or coins dropping into a metal change tray, or the particular ratcheting song of a typewriter carriage returning home. Nobody killed those sounds. They simply stopped being made, the way words stop being spoken.

Her favorite acquisition is nine seconds long: a telephone book being opened. The pages don't rustle so much as exhale. The book belonged to a plumber named Gus, seventy-eight years old, who kept every edition since 1962 in his garage, and when Mira found him he insisted on reading her his own listing aloud, as if introducing himself formally after all these years.

"Gus Kowalczyk," he said. "That's me."

"That's you," she said, and pressed record.

What she cannot explain to the grant committee is why any of this matters. Her reports ask for cultural significance, so she writes *documenting vernacular soundscapes* and *preserving intangible heritage*. But the truth is stranger. The truth is that she believes people are made partly of sound—that somewhere inside each of us is a small orchestra performing only the music we heard in childhood, and when those sounds vanish from the world, something in us loses its tuning fork.

Her father was an engineer on the old coastal freight line, and she grew up falling asleep to the midnight train, its long low note coming through her bedroom wall like a hand smoothing her hair. The line closed when she was nineteen. She can still hear the train. That is the problem—or the miracle, depending on the day. The sound outlived its source inside her skull, and no archive can hold that version of it. She has tried. She once recorded the whistle of a museum's restored locomotive, played it back in her car, and felt nothing but the flat disappointment of looking at a photograph of someone you love. The image is accurate and the person is missing.

Last month she got a call from a nursing home outside Dayton. A resident there, a ninety-four-year-old woman named Eleanor, claimed to be the last living switchboard operator in the state, and wanted to give the archive "the sound of connecting people" before she died. Mira drove out and set up in a sunroom full of plastic plants. They had borrowed a board from a museum. Eleanor's hands shook above it—but when she touched the cords, when she took the call and plugged it through and said her crisp old question, *Number, please*, her voice changed entirely. Steady. Younger. For six seconds she was not a woman in a sunroom; she was a node in the nervous system of an entire town, feeling everyone's voices pass through her fingers.

Mira got it all on tape. Then Eleanor looked up and said, quietly, that what she missed wasn't really the board. It was the sound the office made at night. All those lines humming at once, hundreds of open circuits carrying nothing—waiting. Like the building was breathing.

Mira recorded the restored switchboard's idle hum anyway. It wasn't the same. Of course it wasn't.

On the drive home she thought about what her father used to say when she asked what he listened for on long runs. *Mostly,* he said, *I listen for what shouldn't be there. A knock in the engine. Silence where the wind ought to be. You spend your whole life learning a sound, and what you're really learning is how it breaks.*

Maybe that's the actual job, Mira thinks, unlocking the basement door again, flicking the switches that bring the shelves of tape and drives up to temperature. Not preserving sounds. Preserving the knowledge of how they break—and the strange human faith that if we keep enough of them, carefully labeled and dated, then someday someone will press play and be handed back a piece of the world, still warm, still running on time.

There is one more thing she has never submitted for the catalogue, though it may be the most important recording she owns. It was made the week her father died, on her phone, by accident. She had called his number intending to leave a message telling him the hospice schedule, forgetting for one ring that no one would answer. The outgoing greeting was his voice—*You've reached the Kowalczyks, leave it after the beep*—recorded decades earlier, back when the answering machine was new and he'd made the whole family listen to his takes. After the beep, her own breath catching. Ten seconds total.

She plays it sometimes, late, in the basement, with the levels checked and the room silent. Not because the archive needs it.

Because some sounds are not disappearing from the world. They are just moving somewhere no microphone has ever been able to follow—and the least she can do, professionally speaking, is stand at the edge of that country taking notes.

Upstairs, the library hums. She sets down her bag, checks the meters, and waits for whatever comes next to make its sound.
